column2: Lung-protective ventilation uses 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight: 6 × 59 ≈ 354 mL, with plateau pressure ≤ 30 cmH2O.
Hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae 24–72 h after a long-bone fracture is fat embolism syndrome; supportive care, early fixation prevents it.
Berlin ARDS criteria: onset < 1 week, bilateral opacities, not cardiac, PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 300 on PEEP ≥ 5. Respiratory rate is not a criterion.
Acute type 2 failure with relative bradycardia after trauma suggests a high cervical cord injury (C3–C5) paralysing the diaphragm; immobilise and image.
Lobar collapse causes a shunt with normal/low PaCO2 (type 1). Flail chest, OSA, myasthenia and opioids cause hypoventilation (type 2).
Acute respiratory acidosis with a normal A–a gradient (~7 mmHg) means pure hypoventilation, e.g. opioid overdose: give naloxone.
In MND, NIV is offered when symptoms of hypoventilation (orthopnoea, poor sleep, morning headache, breathlessness) accompany hypercapnia.
High-flow oxygen caused CO2 narcosis; stuporous with acidosis and worsening hypoxia, he cannot protect his airway: intubate and ventilate.
Exudate-filled alveoli are perfused but not ventilated (true shunt), so hypoxaemia barely improves with high FiO2; PEEP recruits them.
Nephrotic syndrome causes a transudate (low oncotic pressure); pneumonia, malignancy and infarction cause exudates.
Recurrent high fever with rigors and pleuritic pain weeks after pneumonia is empyema; aspirate (pH < 7.2, pus) and drain.
Purulent fluid with pH < 7.2, glucose < 3.3 mmol/L and neutrophils is empyema: chest drain plus antibiotics.
Empyema follows pneumonia, TB, infected haemothorax, surgery, oesophageal rupture or subphrenic abscess; rheumatic fever is not a cause.
Stony dullness and a dense homogeneous opacity after blunt chest trauma is a haemothorax.
Traumatic haemothorax: left chest drain in the safe triangle; > 1500 mL initially or ~200 mL/h ongoing indicates thoracotomy.
Sudden pleuritic pain in a tall young athlete with hyper-resonance and reduced expansion is primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
A large left effusion with a week of fever and pleuritic pain in a heavy drinker is most likely empyema; aspirate urgently.
Homogeneous lower-zone opacity with a meniscus and lost costophrenic angle is a pleural effusion; unilateral with normal LV needs investigation.
Unilateral effusion with normal LV function: bedside ultrasound and diagnostic aspiration; no need to stop apixaban (BTS 2023).
A visible pleural edge with no markings beyond and a hyperlucent hemithorax is a left pneumothorax.
In a cannabis smoker, a large bulla can mimic pneumothorax; CT distinguishes them before any drain (risk of bronchopleural fistula).
Asbestos, cytology-negative exudate and circumferential thickening suggest mesothelioma; thoracoscopic biopsy (yield > 90%).
Hypothyroidism can cause a transudate; infarction, RA, TB and drugs cause exudates.
Light's exudate criteria: protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, or fluid LDH > 2/3 of the upper limit of serum LDH.
A septated effusion with fever means complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema: pH < 7.2 (here 6.9) with low glucose and high LDH.
If needle aspiration fails to re-expand the lung, insert a chest drain (or ambulatory device); stop aspiration at 2.5 L.
In poorly draining pleural infection, intrapleural alteplase plus DNase improves drainage and reduces surgery (MIST-2).
Sudden hypotension, high airway pressure and absent breath sounds in a ventilated patient is tension pneumothorax: needle decompression.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion: loculation, pus, positive Gram stain/culture, pH < 7.2 or glucose < 3.3 mmol/L. Reaccumulation alone is not one.
The fluid is a lymphocytic exudate (protein ratio 0.8, LDH ratio 0.89); cirrhosis causes a transudate, so it is not the cause.
Recurrent primary pneumothorax is treated by VATS pleurectomy/abrasion (recurrence 1–5%); stopping smoking cuts recurrence.
Protein separates transudate from exudate (ratio > 0.5, or > 35 g/L); Light's criteria are used when protein is 25–35 g/L.
A new effusion with ongoing sepsis during pneumonia: ultrasound-guided diagnostic tap; pH < 7.2 or pus means a drain.
Remove a pneumothorax drain only when bubbling has stopped and the lung is re-expanded; never clamp a bubbling drain.
Sudden breathlessness and desaturation during subclavian line insertion is iatrogenic pneumothorax; urgent CXR.
Hypotension and tracheal deviation away from a silent hemithorax is tension pneumothorax: immediate large-bore cannula decompression.
Stony dullness, reduced breath sounds and fremitus with the trachea pushed away is a large effusion (TB or malignancy here).
All Light's criteria negative (protein 0.38, LDH 0.46, LDH < 127): a transudate, most commonly heart failure.
Pneumothorax: hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds on the affected side, with a large one pushing the trachea away.
Smoking (including cannabis) is the main modifiable risk for pneumothorax recurrence: advise stopping.
A lymphocytic sterile exudate with a 3-month history in an older woman suggests malignancy (lung cancer); cytology and CT.
Recurrent right pneumothorax within 72 h of menstruation is catamenial pneumothorax from thoracic endometriosis.
Symptomatic primary pneumothorax without high-risk features, wishing to avoid admission: ambulatory valve device (BTS 2023).
Secondary pneumothorax in COPD is high-risk; symptomatic or > 2 cm needs admission and a chest drain.
Photosensitive rash, arthralgia and pleural effusion suggest SLE serositis; check ANA, anti-dsDNA and complement.
Pneumothorax with cyanosis, hypotension and tracheal deviation away is tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then drain.
Rheumatoid effusions are exudates with very low glucose and pH, mimicking empyema; new polyarthritis reveals the diagnosis.
Dry cough, progressive dyspnoea, clubbing, Velcro crackles and hypoxaemia in an older adult is IPF; HRCT for UIP pattern.
